"executive_summary": "This paper investigates whether giant planets can form at close distances to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of circumstellar discs. Two main theories of giant planet formation exist: core accretion, which is slow and may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs, and gravitational fragmentation, which operates on a fast dynamical timescale. Gravitational fragmentation requires two conditions: the disc must be gravitationally unstable (Toomre parameter Q <~ 1), and it must cool fast enough for compressional energy to be radiated away on a dynamical timescale (tCOOL < C(γ) tORB). Previous hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results, largely due to different treatments of radiative transfer. The authors develop a new method to treat the energy equation and equation of state in smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, accounting for radiative transfer effects, including the different chemical and internal states of hydrogen and dust properties at varying densities and temperatures. They simulate a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending from 2 to 40 AU, in two cases: one with only a background radiation field of 10 K, and one with additional heating from the central star. In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, it cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~ 2 tORB throughout the disc). In the second case, although it can cool fast enough to fragment at radii >~ 20 AU, it is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~ 1.5). The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~ 50 AU. Their results corroborate those of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), who used a different treatment for radiative transfer. The paper also validates their numerical scheme against analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) and compares with previous simulations. The implications are significant for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~ 100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. This work reinforces the view that core accretion, rather than gravitational fragmentation, is the dominant mechanism for giant planet formation at close distances to solar-type stars.",

summary.title: Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs? Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: planetary system and protoplanetary disc formation
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates whether giant planets can form at close distances to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of circumstellar discs. Two main theories of giant planet formation exist: core accretion, which is slow and may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs, and gravitational fragmentation, which operates on a fast dynamical timescale. Gravitational fragmentation requires two conditions: the disc must be gravitationally unstable (Toomre parameter Q <~ 1), and it must cool fast enough for compressional energy to be radiated away on a dynamical timescale (tCOOL < C(γ) tORB). Previous hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results, largely due to different treatments of radiative transfer. The authors develop a new method to treat the energy equation and equation of state in smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, accounting for radiative transfer effects, including the different chemical and internal states of hydrogen and dust properties at varying densities and temperatures. They simulate a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending from 2 to 40 AU, in two cases: one with only a background radiation field of 10 K, and one with additional heating from the central star. In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, it cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~ 2 tORB throughout the disc). In the second case, although it can cool fast enough to fragment at radii >~ 20 AU, it is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~ 1.5). The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~ 50 AU. Their results corroborate those of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), who used a different treatment for radiative transfer. The paper also validates their numerical scheme against analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) and compares with previous simulations. The implications are significant for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~ 100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. This work reinforces the view that core accretion, rather than gravitational fragmentation, is the dominant mechanism for giant planet formation at close distances to solar-type stars.

The disc cannot cool fast enough to fragment under low background heating.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates whether giant planets can form at close distances to solar-type stars through gravitational fragmentation of circumstellar discs. Two main theories of giant planet formation exist: core accretion, which is slow and may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs, and gravitational fragmentation, which operates on a fast dynamical timescale. Gravitational fragmentation requires two conditions: the disc must be gravitationally unstable (Toomre parameter Q <~ 1), and it must cool fast enough for compressional energy to be radiated away on a dynamical timescale (tCOOL < C(γ) tORB). Previous hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results, largely due to different treatments of radiative transfer. The authors develop a new method to treat the energy equation and equation of state in smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, accounting for radiative transfer effects, including the different chemical and internal states of hydrogen and dust properties at varying densities and temperatures. They simulate a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending from 2 to 40 AU, in two cases: one with only a background radiation field of 10 K, and one with additional heating from the central star. In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, it cannot cool fast enough (cooling time >~ 2 tORB throughout the disc). In the second case, although it can cool fast enough to fragment at radii >~ 20 AU, it is not gravitationally unstable (Q >~ 1.5). The authors conclude that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~ 50 AU. Their results corroborate those of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), who used a different treatment for radiative transfer. The paper also validates their numerical scheme against analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) and compares with previous simulations. The implications are significant for understanding hot Jupiter formation, as fragmentation at large radii (>~ 100 AU) would produce objects unlikely to migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. This work reinforces the view that core accretion, rather than gravitational fragmentation, is the dominant mechanism for giant planet formation at close distances to solar-type stars.

Research Context
Giant planets are found very close to their central stars on eccentric orbits. Two main theories of giant planet formation have been proposed. Core accretion is slow and may exceed the lifetime of circumstellar discs. Gravitational fragmentation operates on a fast dynamical timescale. Gravitational fragmentation requires the disc to be gravitationally unstable. Gravitational fragmentation requires the disc to cool fast enough. Previous hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results. The contradictions arise mainly from different treatments of radiative transfer. The cooling condition requires the cooling time to be less than a critical multiple of the orbital period. The critical cooling coefficient C(γ) depends on the adiabatic exponent.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs in the inner region? Whether disc fragmentation can function in the inner region of real discs is debatable. The study aims to investigate the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation. The disc must be gravitationally unstable for fragmentation to occur. The disc must cool fast enough for fragmentation to occur. The disc cooling must happen on a dynamical timescale. The critical cooling coefficient C(γ) is predicted to be between 0.5 and 2.0. The authors hypothesize that discs cannot cool fast enough close to the central star. The authors hypothesize that stellar irradiation stabilizes the disc against fragmentation. The authors predict that fragmentation is unlikely at radii <~ 50 AU.

Methodological Details
The simulations use the SPH code dragon. The code invokes an octal tree to compute gravity and find neighbours. The code uses adaptive smoothing lengths. The code uses multiple particle timesteps. The artificial viscosity parameters are α = 0.1 and β = 0.2. The Balsara switch is used in the artificial viscosity. A second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme is used. The energy equation is treated with the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007). The method accounts for compressional heating. The method accounts for viscous heating. The method accounts for radiation heating from the background. The method accounts for radiation cooling. The method implicitly accounts for radiation heating from the particle's neighbourhood. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. The equation of state accounts for rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen. The equation of state accounts for the different chemical states of hydrogen and helium. The effects of H2 dissociation are included in the equation of state. The effects of H0 ionisation are included in the equation of state. The first and second ionisation of He are included in the equation of state. The temperatures in the simulations are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate. Contributions from metals are ignored in the simulations. The mean molecular weight µ is constant in the simulations. The opacity is parameterized by Bell & Lin (1994). The opacity parameterization is κ(ρ, T) = κ0 ρa T b. The opacity changes due to ice mantle melting are taken into account. The opacity changes due to dust sublimation are taken into account. The opacity changes due to molecular and H− contributions are taken into account. The code has been extensively tested in previous work. The code reproduces the detailed 3D results of Masunaga & Inutsuka (2000). The code reproduces the analytic test of Spiegel (1957). The simulations model a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star. The disc is relatively massive and has been observed in the Orion Nebula cluster. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density profile is Σ(R) ~ R−1/2. The initial temperature profile is T(R) ~ R−1. The initial surface density parameter Σ0 is 1.6 × 10^3 g cm−2. The temperature at R ~ 1 AU is T0 = 1200 K. The asymptotic temperature far from the central star is T∞ = 10 K. The initial disc thickness is calculated by balancing gravitational and pressure forces. The local sound speed is c2(R) = kT(R)/(µmp). The simulations use 2 × 10^5 SPH particles to represent the disc. In both cases the disc relaxes from the initial conditions to a quasi-steady state. Each plot of the evolution contains 5 lines corresponding to different instances. The instances correspond to times t = 500, 1000, ..., 2500 yr. The initial conditions match those of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The computations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility. The work was supported by PPARC grant PP/E000967/1.

Procedures And Architectures
The energy equation method performs well in the optically thin regime. The energy equation method performs well in the optically thick regime. The energy equation method is efficient and relatively easy to implement. The equation of state includes the effects of H2 dissociation. The equation of state includes the effects of H0 ionisation. The equation of state includes the first and second ionisation of He. The dust and gas opacity uses the parameterization by Bell & Lin (1994). The opacity parameterization is κ(ρ, T) = κ0 ρa T b. The opacity changes due to ice mantle melting are taken into account. The opacity changes due to dust sublimation are taken into account. The opacity changes due to molecular and H− contributions are taken into account. The new method allows for the first time radiative hydrodynamic simulations of discs. The radiative scheme allows for irradiation of the disc by the central star. The first simulation uses a constant background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. The second simulation uses radiation from the central star with TBGR ~ R−1. The disc relaxes to a quasi-steady state in both cases. The disc evolution is plotted over time for both cases. The disc relaxes to a lower-temperature quasi-steady state without stellar irradiation. The disc reaches a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr under low background heating. The Toomre parameter is calculated using the surface density and midplane disc temperature. The temperature and cooling time are additionally averaged vertically relative to the disc midplane. The first simulation was repeated using a smaller number of SPH particles. The smaller simulation used 5 × 10^4 SPH particles. The vertical temperature profile is compared with the analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990). The Hubeny (1990) calculation studies the vertical structure of a cylindrically symmetric stationary Keplerian disc. The Hubeny (1990) calculation treats radiation transport only in the vertical direction. The Hubeny (1990) calculation neglects the self-gravity of the disc. The Hubeny (1990) calculation neglects convection and external irradiation. The comparison with Hubeny (1990) uses a snapshot of the disc at t = 2000 yr. The second simulation assumes the background temperature is TBGR(R) = (T0^2 (R/AU)^−2 + T∞^2)^1/2. The results of the second simulation are shown in Figs. 9-14. The initial conditions of the disc are closer to equilibrium in the second simulation. The temperature of the disc remains almost constant in the second simulation. The disc is overall hotter in the second simulation due to heating from the central star.

Key Results
The disc does not fragment in the case with only background heating. The disc cannot cool fast enough in the case with only background heating. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the case with stellar heating. The disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU under low background heating. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~ 2 tORB under low background heating. Weak spiral arms form in the disc but do not show any tendency to fragment. The disc relaxes to a lower-temperature quasi-steady state without stellar irradiation. The disc can cool fast enough to fragment at radii >~ 20 AU with stellar heating. The disc is not gravitationally unstable with Q >~ 1.5 with stellar heating. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms with stellar heating. The temperatures calculated are ~15% higher than those of Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures are less than 3% higher than those of Cai et al. (2007). The spiral arms in our simulation are weaker than those of Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures calculated are generally larger than those of Boley et al. (2006). The differences at large radii are attributable to using a different background radiation field. The differences at small radii could be due to higher viscous heating in our simulations. The Toomre parameter in our simulation is generally higher than that of Boley et al. (2006). The cooling times in our simulation are lower than those of Boley et al. (2006). The results of our simulation are more comparable to those of Cai et al. (2007). The strength of the spiral arms in our simulation is similar to that of Cai et al. (2007). Our temperature profiles are similar to those predicted by Hubeny (1990). There are some deviations at larger distances from the central star at low optical depths. The adiabatic index is γ = 5/3 outside ~10 AU where the temperature is less than ~80 K. The adiabatic index is γ = 7/5 closer to the central star where the temperature is higher. The cooling time is always >~ 2 tORB within ~30 AU. The disc is gravitationally unstable at R ~ 20-30 AU under external radiation field of 10 K. The disc does not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough under external radiation field of 10 K. The heating from the central star stabilizes the disc against fragmentation. Discs are even less prone to fragment in their inner regions when stellar irradiation is taken into account. Gas giant planets probably cannot form close to the central star by gravitational fragmentation of discs. The results corroborate those of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The results are similar despite using different treatments for radiative transfer and hydrodynamics.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The disc cannot cool fast enough in the case with only background heating. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~ 2 tORB under low background heating. The disc is not gravitationally unstable in the case with stellar heating. The heating from the central star stabilizes the disc against fragmentation. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms with stellar heating. The results agree with previous simulations of discs heated by envelope radiation. Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~ 50 AU. 2. The strongest evidence is that the disc does not fragment in both cases, because it cannot cool fast enough or it is not gravitationally unstable. 3. The future path is to investigate the formation of giant planets at larger radii (>~ 100 AU) where fragmentation is possible.
